sections.heading: A school-based entry point
paragraphs: The Department of School Education and Literacy’s Special Campaign 6 links cleaner campuses with responsible e-waste management. This creates a practical setting in which students and staff can connect environmental learning with disposal behaviour.

The mechanism is behavioural and institutional: awareness may improve segregation and collection, while designated channels can reduce unsafe disposal. However, a collection event alone does not establish that waste was safely recycled.

sections.heading: From campaign activity to verified outcomes
paragraphs: Effective implementation requires safe temporary storage, documented handover and use of authorised processing channels. The E-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 support formal registration and record-based accountability for relevant entities.[1]
The broader lesson is that school campaigns should be assessed by traceable downstream outcomes, not only by the number of awareness activities conducted.

advisory_notes: The proposed GS3.5 anchor is strong; GS2.6 and GS2.5 are defensible but secondary because the release is primarily environmental governance and education administration.
The static definition of e-waste management and the circular-economy framing are background analysis, not claims established by the PIB release; retain them but label them as contextual explanation.
The statement that the Rules provide registration for manufacturers, producers, refurbishers and recyclers is supported by the official rules, which apply from 1 April 2023.[1]
The claim that authorised channels reduce unsafe disposal is a reasonable mechanism, but it should be framed as a potential outcome rather than an assured result.
The background says the Rules apply to specified equipment and entities; specify that the Rules do not regulate every discarded electronic item or every institution in identical ways.
The recall card’s phrase “connects ... with responsible e-waste management” is accurate, but “implemented by” should not imply that every school nationwide carried out the same activities.
The pocketRead headline and deck are supported by the supplied PIB extract; the two explanatory paragraphs appropriately distinguish collection activity from verified recycling.
The hypothetical school example is correctly labelled as an illustration and should remain clearly separate from the reported Kartavya Bhavan mural and bins.

Integrate responsible consumption, repair, reuse and material recovery into age-appropriate environmental education.
